What would it take to get back in? Making some of the older, usually hard to get items more accessible. Things like the Mount drops from previous raids or instances (Baron's mount anyone?) A better way to centralize the player base of servers/mixed servers and a way to promote players in these zones to interact. They introduced a Pokemon like mini game for christs sake, that's pretty lame. Introduce a duel mini game system, where players have set gear for duels (that doesn't take up inventory space and is automatically equipped at the start of a duel).

A 'hardcore PvP' zone would be awesome, where the zone is permanent PvP, and similar to the previous duel idea, you start with set items (again, no inven space and automatically equipped upon entering) that can only be replaced with items earned within the hardcore zone.

The zone will incorporate all skills your character currently has with some extra recipes specific to the zone. The hardcore part comes in that when you die, you reset your items (keep recipes for skills though, perhaps). Make it either FFA or Faction based. To prevent mega trolling you can leave the zone instantly when not in combat (allowing players to zone in and out without travel time) and access the zone via a spell so you travel there from anywhere in the game world. When you zone out you return to where you zoned in from and when you zone in you spawn in a random location.

Within the zone you can 'lock' players to your character. When you lock a player, that players name will appear on your screen when they are also in the zone you are in. By clicking on that players name you can port to them (when not in combat) allowing small groups to band together and zone in/out at will without breaking consistency too much. You'll have a limit on how many players you can lock within the zone, and not all friends will appear on this list.

You could re-use existing portions of the world map to prevent having to make an all new zone. Imagine if it rotated through a handful of existing zones on a weekly basis, keeping it fresh each week and providing incentive to clock in.

Now that your little fort place can gather resources etc for you the need for endless farming has decreased significantly. This'll provide a new active way for everyone from casuals to serious players a new adventure within the game. Mobs would be on short respawn timers to ensure the zone stays active, perhaps with spawns blocked within a certain distance of players. This'll promote movement within the zone without large periods of blank space and also prevent spawn farming of sought after mobs.

There are no objectives, such as mini-raid the Alliance/Horde base as the zone is decentralized. Your regular towns still exist though as neutral trade centers instead of their vanilla form. You'll be able to do all your repairs etc at these locations, but npc's are not attackable (to prevent town wipe trolling) and only provide minor services. Think of it as bare bones.

Items could work in many ways. Each class and/or race combination starts with a specific set of base items. Your items could level up as you utilize them and may be boosted using some skills. To max items out you'll have to complete quests or objectives which may require specific zones to do, enticing you to check which zones are available.

Each individual player could receive a number of weekly objectives to complete based on their race, class or skills. It could be anything from 'slay X opponents' to 'perform X healing to friendly players' (overhealing not included). When you complete objectives you might be rewarded with 'Item Points' which could be spent to level up your gear as mentioned previously.

I was thinking about the open source movement for software, but I had never considered it for ISPs or hardware manufacturing.

What would be the purpose of installing an open source operating system on a phone if the hardware itself wasn't open, more so, how could you protect your privacy/freedom if the mobile phone itself was connected to a network run by a government/company?

I'm not so much talking about the practical concerns of implementing this idea, though that may be why I had never considered it, but nonetheless, it's interesting to think that the open source movement for technology is mostly software oriented, while the infrastructure/hardware needed to support the software itself is not.
Is there an Open Source movement for hardware/infrastructure?

Open hardware is a thing. Look up Arduino.

Also here:

http://www.ladyada.net/library/openhardware/whatisit.html

At the end of the day, though, Arduino is still pretty tied to Atmel's architecture. If you're looking for truly open hardware, you're looking at FPGA designs, which all rest on an IEEE-specified layer of Verilog that works for all vendors' FPGAs.

With hardware, it depends on how you define "Open Source". Full datasheet and functional diagrams? Sure, most companies provide these things anyway. Actual schematics that are more than just IO diagrams? Not so much. As FourNomalCents said, FPGAs are the closest thing right now to truly open hardware, considering the user needs to know what the hardware layout is to actually use the board.

As for your example with mobile phones, it's the nature of the technology that makes it vulnerable to spying. There's a concept that's been floating around for quite some time now, called Darknet (or Meshnet). The ultimate goal of a darknet is to provide an alternative network to the ones that are commercially available, with one's data and anonymity preserved by the same mechanism that protects the network from government infiltration; localization. There are types of mesh networks already available (such as DC++) that do this exact thing. There are also special routers and DIY servers that prevent others from simply snooping on your LAN/Wifi.

While I dont have much to add to this conversation, I do support the question and the notion.

We need trully open hardware in order to 'own' and trust our devices.
